evidence: Receiving DO2 sensor at t=52.0 h: 3.695 mg/L, after collapse from 10.66 mg/L at t=50.0 h (sudden step drop starting t=50.2)
Minimum DO constraint is 2.0 mg/L; extrapolation reaches it in ~3-4 h under KEEP
Source batches (source-1,2,3) at t=52 h show DO2 ~10.5-11.5 mg/L, confirming receiving deviation is abnormal
Receiving P assay (delayed) t=48 h: 2.80 g/L and rising - production mass retained, stop rejected
Allowed action bounds: combined = feed 0.8, air 1.15, within permitted ranges
args.rationale: The receiving fermentation shows an abrupt DO2 collapse from ~10.7 mg/L at t=50.0 h to 3.7 mg/L at t=52.0 h (falling ~0.5 mg/L/h), unlike source batches which held ~10.5-11.5 mg/L at the same age. If DO2 continues at this slope it breaches the 2.0 mg/L minimum within ~3-4 h. increase_air alone (max 1.15x) directly raises oxygen transfer and is the fastest way to lift DO2 above the constraint; the 0.8x feed reduction reduces oxygen demand so the DO recovery is sustained and does not rely solely on the bounded air increase. The 20% feed cut retains most production capacity (P was still rising, 2.80 g/L at t=48 assay), unlike a stop (zero counted production) or a strong 40% feed cut. KEEP alone carries a high probability of an oxygen-constraint violation. Combined bounded intervention best balances constraint safety with product-mass retention.
args.uncertainty: Exact air-transfer gain from 1.15x air and the kinetics of demand reduction from a 0.8x feed cut are unknown (hidden parameters), so the speed of DO2 recovery is uncertain; the DO2 drop could also partly reflect viscosity or mixing effects that air increase only partially offsets. The 48-h P assay lags current state by 4 h, so true current titer is uncertain. If the collapse were a sensor artifact, the feed reduction would cost some productivity - but the consistent multi-point decline (10 points over 1.8 h) makes artifact unlikely.
